text: --- Source: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) URL: https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/diagnosis Title: Anemia - Diagnosis AccessDate: 2026-10-10 --- Anemia occurs when the blood lacks enough healthy red blood cells. Hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. A primary marker for anemia is low hemoglobin levels. Typical adult reference ranges are 14-17 gm/dL for men and 12-15 gm/dL for women.
title: Anemia - Diagnosis & Markers
organization: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)

text: --- Source: National Library of Medicine (MedlinePlus) / NHLBI URL: https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/ Title: Complete Blood Count (CBC) Reference Guide AccessDate: 2026-10-11 --- # Complete Blood Count (CBC) A complete blood count (CBC) is a common blood test that evaluates overall health and detects a wide range of disorders, including anemia, infection, and leukemia. ## 1. Key Components and Typical Reference Ranges - **Red Blood Cells (RBC)**: Carry oxygen from the lungs to the body. - Typical adult male: 4.5 to 5.9 million cells/mcL (or 10^12/L). - Typical adult female: 4.1 to 5.1 million cells/mcL. - Low RBC: May indicate anemia, bleeding, or nutritional deficiency. - High RBC (erythrocytosis): May occur in dehydration, chronic low oxygen states, or polycythemia vera. - **Hemoglobin (Hb / Hgb)**: The oxygen-carrying iron-rich protein in red blood cells. - Typical adult male: 13.8 to 17.2 g/dL. - Typical adult female: 12.1 to 15.1 g/dL. - Low Hemoglobin: Common indicator of anemia, blood loss, kidney disease, or bone marrow issues. - High Hemoglobin: May indicate smoking, high altitude living, heart disease, or polycythemia. - **Hematocrit (Hct)**: The

Range: 80 to 100 fL. - Low MCV (<80 fL): Microcytic anemia (most commonly iron deficiency anemia or thalassemia). - High MCV (>100 fL): Macrocytic anemia (commonly vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, thyroid issues, or liver disease). - **MCH (Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin)**: Average amount of hemoglobin inside a red cell. Types & Characteristics - Type 1: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction, absolute insulin deficiency. Often onset <35 years, lower BMI, rapid onset. - Type 2: Progressive loss of beta-cell secretion + insulin resistance. Often adult onset, associated with obesity. - Gestational (GDM): Glucose intolerance first recognized during pregnancy (24-28 weeks). - Monogenic: Single gene mutation (e.g., MODY). ## 2. Symptoms of Hyperglycemia - Polyuria (Excessive urination) - Polydipsia (Excessive thirst) - Unexplained weight loss - Other: Blurred vision, fatigue, poor wound healing. ## 3. text: --- Source: American Heart Association (AHA) / MedlinePlus URL: https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/cholesterol-levels/ Title: Lipid Panel & Cholesterol Reference Guide AccessDate: 2026-10-11 --- # Lipid Panel & Cholesterol Guidelines A lipid panel measures fats (lipids) in the blood to evaluate cardiovascular risk, including coronary artery disease, heart attack, and stroke. ## 1. Key Lipid Markers & Target Ranges (Adults) - **Total Cholesterol**: Combined measurement of LDL, HDL, and other lipid components. - Desirable: Less than 200 mg/dL (or <5.2 mmol/L). - Borderline high: 200 to 239 mg/dL. - High: 240 mg/dL or higher. - **Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL) Cholesterol ("Bad" Cholesterol)**: Carries cholesterol to tissues; excess contributes to atherosclerotic plaque buildup. - Optimal: Less than 100 mg/dL (<2.6 mmol/L). - Near optimal: 100 to 129 mg/dL. - Borderline high: 130 to 159 mg/dL. - High: 160 to 189 mg/dL. - Very high: 190 mg/dL or above. - **High-Density Lipoprotein (HDL) Cholesterol ("Good" Cholesterol)**: Transports cholesterol away from arteries back to the liver for excretion. - Optimal (protective): 60 mg/dL or higher. - Acceptable for men: 40 to 59 mg/dL. - Acceptabl
title: Lipid Panel & Cholesterol Reference Guide

text: esterol ("Good" Cholesterol)**: Transports cholesterol away from arteries back to the liver for excretion. - Optimal (protective): 60 mg/dL or higher. - Acceptable for men: 40 to 59 mg/dL. - Acceptable for women: 50 to 59 mg/dL. - Low (risk factor): Less than 40 mg/dL in men; less than 50 mg/dL in women. - **Triglycerides**: Most common type of fat stored in the body, derived from excess dietary calories. - Normal: Less than 150 mg/dL (<1.7 mmol/L). - Borderline high: 150 to 199 mg/dL. - High: 200 to 499 mg/dL. - Very high: 500 mg/dL or higher (carries risk of acute pancreatitis). ## 2. Lifestyle and Clinical Considerations - Elevated triglycerides and LDL, combined with low HDL, increase atherosclerosis risk. - Fasting for 9-12 hours is traditionally recommended prior to drawing a lipid panel, although non-fasting panels are increasingly utilized for standard screening.

text: --- Source: American Liver Foundation / MedlinePlus URL: https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/liver-function-tests/ Title: Liver Function Tests (Hepatic Function Panel) AccessDate: 2026-10-11 --- # Liver Function Tests (Hepatic Panel) Liver function tests (LFTs) measure specific proteins, liver enzymes, and bilirubin in the blood to evaluate hepatic health, detect liver damage, or monitor treatment response. ## 1. Key Liver Enzymes - **Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT)**: Enzyme found mainly in hepatocytes (liver cells). Most specific marker for liver injury. - Typical adult range: 7 to 56 U/L. - Markedly high ALT (>5-10x upper limit): Acute viral hepatitis, toxic drug injury (e.g., acetaminophen overdose), or ischemic liver injury. - Moderately high ALT: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), chronic hepatitis, or alcohol-related liver injury. - **Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST)**: Enzyme found in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, and kidneys. - Typical adult range: 10 to 40 U/L. - AST to ALT ratio (De Ritis ratio): A ratio >2:1 is frequently observed in alcoholic liver disease. - **Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)**: Enzyme associated with the biliary tract and bones. - Typical adult range

text: ALT ratio (De Ritis ratio): A ratio >2:1 is frequently observed in alcoholic liver disease. - **Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)**: Enzyme associated with the biliary tract and bones. - Typical adult range: 44 to 147 U/L. - Elevated ALP: Bile duct obstruction, gallstones, cholestasis, or rapid bone turnover/disease. ## 2. Bilirubin Markers - **Total Bilirubin**: Yellow-orange byproduct of normal hemoglobin breakdown. - Typical adult range: 0.1 to 1.2 mg/dL. - Elevated Bilirubin (>2.0 - 2.5 mg/dL): Leads to clinical jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes). - **Direct (Conjugated) Bilirubin**: 0.0 to 0.3 mg/dL. High levels suggest biliary excretion impairment or hepatitis.

text: --- Source: National Library of Medicine (MedlinePlus) / National Kidney Foundation URL: https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp/ Title: Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) & Kidney Function AccessDate: 2026-10-11 --- # Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) A Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) is a blood test measuring 14 different substances to evaluate body metabolism, kidney function, liver health, fluid and electrolyte balance, and blood sugar. ## 1. Kidney & Waste Markers - **Serum Creatinine**: Waste product produced by muscle breakdown and filtered by healthy kidneys. - Typical adult range: 0.7 to 1.3 mg/dL for men; 0.6 to 1.1 mg/dL for women. - Elevated Creatinine: Indicates reduced kidney filtration, acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease (CKD), dehydration, or high muscle breakdown. - **Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)**: Waste product from protein digestion processed by the liver and removed by the kidneys. - Typical adult range: 7 to 20 mg/dL. - Elevated BUN: Dehydration, high protein diet, kidney dysfunction, or gastrointestinal bleeding. - **Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR)**: Calculated metric estimating kidney filtering capacity.

Electrolytes and Fluid Balance - **Sodium (Na)**: 135 to 145 mEq/L (or mmol/L). Regulates fluid balance and nerve transmission. - Hyponatremia (<135): Water retention, diuretic medications, heart failure. - Hypernatremia (>145): Dehydration, excessive sodium intake. - **Potassium (K)**: 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L (or mmol/L). Vital for cardiac rhythm and muscle contraction. - Hypokalemia (<3.5): Diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea; risk of cardiac arrhythmias. - Hyperkalemia (>5.0): Kidney impairment, certain medications; potentially dangerous cardiac arrhythmias. - **Chloride (Cl)**: 96 to 106 mEq/L. Maintains osmotic pressure and acid-base balance. - **Carbon Dioxide / Bicarbonate (CO2 / HCO3)**: 23 to 29 mEq/L. Indicates body acid-base balance. - **Calcium (Ca)**: 8.5 to 10.2 mg/dL. text: --- Source: American Thyroid Association (ATA) / MedlinePlus URL: https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/thyroid-tests/ Title: Thyroid Function Tests Reference Guide AccessDate: 2026-10-11 --- # Thyroid Function Tests Thyroid function tests measure hormones produced by the thyroid gland and pituitary gland to detect hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) or hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid). ## 1. Key Thyroid Markers - **Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH / Thyrotropin)**: Pituitary hormone signaling the thyroid gland to produce thyroid hormones. Primary frontline screening test. - Typical adult range: 0.4 to 4.0 mIU/L (or uIU/mL). - High TSH (>4.0 mIU/L): Primary indicator of hypothyroidism (pituitary produces excess TSH trying to stimulate an underperforming thyroid). Often accompanied by fatigue, weight gain, constipation, and cold intolerance. - Low TSH (<0.4 mIU/L): Primary indicator of hyperthyroidism (pituitary downregulates TSH due to excess circulating thyroid hormone). Often accompanied by weight loss, rapid heart rate (palpitations), anxiety, and heat intolerance. - **Free Thyroxine (Free T4)**: Active, unbound form of the primary hormone made by the thyroid gland. - Typical a
title: Thyroid Function Tests Reference Guide

text: anied by weight loss, rapid heart rate (palpitations), anxiety, and heat intolerance. - **Free Thyroxine (Free T4)**: Active, unbound form of the primary hormone made by the thyroid gland. - Typical adult range: 0.8 to 1.8 ng/dL (10 to 23 pmol/L). - Low Free T4 with High TSH: Confirms overt primary hypothyroidism. - High Free T4 with Low TSH: Confirms overt hyperthyroidism. - Normal Free T4 with High TSH: Subclinical hypothyroidism. - **Free Triiodothyronine (Free T3)**: Active thyroid hormone converted from T4. - Typical adult range: 2.3 to 4.2 pg/mL (3.5 to 6.5 pmol/L).
